Update 11/2/2026 3:00 PM ET: As it turns out, the ultimate parent company and holder of all Tachyum intellectual property is Cayman Islands-based Tachyum Ltd., which controls U.S.-based Tachyum Inc., which in turn controls Slovakia-based Tachyum s.r.o. that is responsible for the lion’s share of Tachyum’s development of the Prodigy universal processor. This means that while Tachyum Inc. and Tachyum s.r.o. can be declared insolvent and liquidated, Tachyum Ltd. can continue operations, establish new entities and continue developing Prodigy.However, the Cayman Islands company holding Prodigy-related patents is itself the target of liquidation proceedings. Therefore, the Slovak subsidiary’s bankruptcy cannot necessarily protect Prodigy’s intellectual property from creditors. If Tachyum Ltd. is liquidated, the control over the Prodigy patents could pass to court-appointed liquidators, who could sell them to repay creditors. While the current Tachyum management could buy Prodigy’s patents back cheaply, they would have to compete with other interested buyers and satisfy the applicable sale requirements. In any case, this could be the end of the road for Tachyum.

Tachyum, the company behind the overpromised and overhyped universal Prodigy processor, has filed for bankruptcy in Bratislava, Slovakia, reports Forbes (as observed by @System360Cheese). The filing follows a court order initiating bankruptcy proceeding after the company repeatedly missed its development and production milestones — but there are still theoretical chances that development of the processor will continue.

Despite eight years of development and numerous promises, Tachyum has yet to demonstrate working Prodigy silicon. Tachyum introduced Prodigy in 2018, targeting a 2019 tape-out and 2020 commercial availability. But the company repeatedly postponed the processor's launch, first to 2021, then to 2022, 2023, 2024, and eventually 2025.

Meanwhile, Prodigy's specifications changed considerably along the line: The original 64-core design evolved into a 128-core processor manufactured on a 5nm-class process technology, then a 192-core chip with 16 DDR5 memory channels. In late 2025, Tachyum announced yet another radical redesign: a chiplet-based architecture with 1,024 cores, 24 DDR5 memory channels, and TDP of 1,600W manufactured using TSMC's 2nm-class node. The redesign would require substantial additional development work and would have delayed commercial availability until 2030 or beyond.

According to court documents cited by Forbes, Tachyum Slovakia itself filed for bankruptcy on October 22, 2026, without waiting for a petition from creditors seeking to recover unpaid debts. The Bratislava III Municipal Court subsequently initiated bankruptcy proceedings after determining that the company's petition met the legal requirements. Under Slovak law, a company that voluntarily files for bankruptcy is presumed insolvent, according to Forbes, so technically Tachyum Slovakia is bankrupt.

If the court formally declares Tachyum bankrupt, a court-appointed trustee will take control of the company's assets, which could then be sold to repay creditors. We do not know at this point what these assets are, but theoretically they may include intellectual property related to its Prodigy processor, patents, and other technologies in addition to hardware used for development. Unless Tachyum secures additional financing or finds a buyer that can fund further development, work on Prodigy could effectively end.

Bankruptcy proceedings against Tachyum's Slovak entity do not necessarily mean that its affiliated companies elsewhere will also cease operations. Furthermore, the company's IP could survive under new ownership (if the company finds a buyer, or transfers IP ownership to another entity), which could theoretically let Prodigy development to continue. Nevertheless, the bankruptcy filing casts serious doubt on Tachyum's ability or intention to bring its long-delayed processor to market.

Theoretically, Tachyum's owners could potentially use bankruptcy proceedings to shed the company's debts, acquire its intellectual property through another legal entity, and resume Prodigy development. There are other options too.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Although most of Tachyum development activities are concentrated in Slovakia, Tachyum Slovakia is a subsidiary of the U.S.-based Tachyum Inc. according to Dennik N. If the American parent company owns the Prodigy IP, while the Slovak subsidiary employs engineers, conducts development, and accumulates debts, bankruptcy could enable the group to eliminate a substantial portion of those liabilities without losing its most valuable technological assets. In short, Tachyum's Slovak subsidiary could disappear along with much of its unpaid debt, while the American parent retains Prodigy IP and attempts to commercialize it somehow in the future. If the Slovak subsidiary owns the IP, the American parent could theoretically buy it from the bankruptcy estate and attempt to commercialize it eventually. Meanwhile, there is another complication: The American parent has reportedly faced pressure from its own creditors, some of whom have requested its liquidation, according to Dennik N. In this case, the destiny of the Prodigy IP is completely unclear.

For now, the future of Prodigy may depend on who actually owns Prodigy's intellectual property — Tachyum Inc. in the U.S. or Tachyum Slovakia — and whether the American subsidiary continues to exist or gets liquidated. The answer could determine whether this bankruptcy represents the end of Prodigy or a restructuring of the Tachyum group with the aim to continue development.

#10530. AI wearables want to remember everything. What happens when we can’t forget?

A growing number of companies are pitching AI hardware products as a remedy for one of humanity’s oldest weaknesses: forgetfulness.

The latest such product comes from Amazon, whose Bee subsidiary introduced a $75 wristband called the Bee Frontier last month. The band, which looks a little like a screen-free fitness tracker, can record meetings and other conversations using two built-in microphones. Frontier owners can then access transcripts and conversation summaries on their phones or computers.

Amazon is also getting ready to sell a Bee phone accessory to keep track of your calls. The company’s pitch for these devices is that they will help you keep track of the many details that would otherwise fall by the wayside, all while safeguarding your privacy with encryption.

Amazon isn’t the only company looking to capture your work and family conversations. In September, Apple unveiled a new feature called Siri Recap for the latest Apple Watch models that can summarize conversations the watch listens in on. A new smart glasses brand called Vonder wants to keep track of your side of every conversation. And a number of work-centric AI recording devices promise to keep track of all your in-office conversations.

To be sure, these gadgets raise privacy concerns. But beyond the fear that any single conversation may be listened in on, there’s a bigger question to consider with the emergence of such devices: How will human interactions change if every word we utter may get sucked up by an AI-powered microphone, to be preserved for eternity?

LED lights alone don’t make devices privacy-friendly

To its credit, Amazon has been trying to address privacy concerns related to Bee products head-on. Audio captured by the devices is processed in real time and then immediately deleted. Transcripts and summaries are processed and stored in an encrypted private compute environment that even Amazon’s own employees can’t access. And any time a Bee device is used to capture a conversation, an LED turns on.

A number of other AI wearables, including Meta’s Ray-Ban AI glasses, also rely on LEDs to signal recording activity to bystanders. But privacy advocates argue that these lights are insufficient.

“That LED light might be known to some people to signify that a camera or a microphone is on and is being used, but not necessarily to every person,” says Electronic Privacy Information Center senior counsel Sara Geoghegan. “It’s small, and people might not notice it.”

Things can get especially dicey in states like California and Florida, which have two-party consent laws that make it illegal to record private conversations without the consent of other participants. Simply having a device signal that it is recording may not be enough to record others legally in those states. “I don’t think that a small LED light on someone’s glasses across from you is consent,” Geoghegan says.

What’s more, some Ray-Ban users have tampered with their LEDs to record others without their knowledge. This reportedly led Meta to remotely disable thousands of glasses.

By and large, companies rely on users of their devices to notify bystanders that they’re being recorded. That can be harder than it sounds, even for well-meaning owners. “Consent is perhaps impossible, if not much more difficult, to obtain from a crowd of people,” Geoghegan argues.

AI recorders could erode public spaces

Not everyone is as worried about the ability of these devices to record people without their knowledge. “I think consent is overvalued,” says Oxford University professor Viktor Mayer-Schönberger, who is instead more concerned about the broader impact of pervasive, AI-powered recording. “The ephemerality of public spaces has evaporated,” he warns.

People used to be able to go to a museum or a bar without worrying that anything and everything they said might get recorded and analyzed. “There used to be a sort of built-in forgetting in public spaces,” Mayer-Schönberger says.

If you made a bad joke or mispronounced a word, chances were that the people around you would forget about it soon after. AI may preserve that remark forever, leading him to wonder: What are the public spaces in which we can just be ourselves without having to worry about repercussions in the future?

Ubiquitous recording could ultimately cause people to retreat from public spaces, much as they frequently do in authoritarian societies. “In liberal democracies, engaging in public spaces is fundamental to the fabric of society,” Mayer-Schönberger says. “That retreat is actually what worries me.”

All of this is further complicated by the fact that some AI devices capture data even when they’re ostensibly not recording. Meta’s Ray-Bans, for instance, can be used to translate the remarks of your conversation partner. While doing so, their LED light stays off, as the devices don’t save any recordings to your phone’s camera roll. However, Meta’s servers may keep transcripts of translated conversations for up to a year if users don’t manually delete them.

The company’s new camera-free AI glasses don’t even have an LED light, making them virtually indistinguishable from regular glasses. “In the future, you will have to assume that everybody who wears glasses is actually recording something,” Mayer-Schönberger says.

AI gadgets require new social norms

AI device makers are aware of people’s privacy concerns, and a few have gone beyond LED lights to address them. HTC’s Vive Eagle smart glasses cease capture when a bystander says “stop recording,” and AI pendant maker Limitless even required audible consent from bystanders before recording their voices when it released its device in 2024. (The company has since been acquired by Meta, which hasn’t adopted this particular feature for its own AI gadgets.)

“Mechanisms and features that can obtain consent should be baked into the technology,” Geoghegan says. “Tech companies absolutely play a role in ensuring that the products they’re selling are safe.”

Mayer-Schönberger agrees that companies should play a more active role, but he also believes the public should have a say in how AI wearables are used. “They require careful negotiations within society of what is permissible and what is not permissible,” he says.

It’s a process he likens to earlier changes in how we behave in public: People used to yell at actors while watching a play, which seems unthinkable nowadays. Conversely, browsing your phone while spending time with others may have seemed strange not too long ago, but is perfectly acceptable to many people today.

“What is really important is that we start negotiating and we start trying things out,” Mayer-Schönberger says. Without public discourse, devices could remain unregulated until something bad happens, at which point regulators will inevitably overreach. “There is no quick fix, so it will be some relatively extreme regulatory theater,” he says. “Think about taking off shoes at airport security on steroids.”

#10528. Shadow ‘accidental landlord’ housing market supply could be looming, says giant institutional landlord

Want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox? Subscribe to the ResiClub newsletter.

Invitation Homes, one of the nation’s largest single-family rental landlords with 85,961 wholly owned homes, says the rental supply picture is improving recently in some markets that have been hardest hit by the multiple-year cyclical cooling that followed the pandemic housing boom. But on its Q3 2026 earnings call on Thursday, management flagged a wild card it’s keeping an eye on: “shadow [SFR] supply.”

Tim Lobner, COO of Invitation Homes, said single-family rental listings from large operators were down 13% year over year in August, including in the company’s three largest markets: Atlanta, Tampa, and Phoenix. Build-to-rent deliveries peaked in 2024 and are expected to keep slowing through 2027 and 2028, he said. And single-family housing starts are forecast to fall 7% this year and another 5% next year, he told analysts.

Invitation Homes says the wild card is so-called shadow rental supply. That includes “accidental landlords,” homeowners who list their homes for sale, can’t get their asking price, and list them for rent instead, along with unsold homebuilder spec homes that could end up in the rental market.

Here’s what Dallas Tanner, CEO of Invitation Homes, said on the company’s October 29, 2026, earnings call:

“In an elevated mortgage rate environment, it [higher rates causing some renters to stay put] is obviously beneficial for our renewals business, but it could bring additional [rental] supply pressure around [on the] new lease side. So we’ll be mindful of that . . . And what do the mom and pops do that are maybe sitting on a home they’re trying to sell? Does that then kind of come back into play as well? So it’s too early to tell on any of those from a supply-oriented story, but it’s something we’re mindful of and we pay attention to.”

And here’s what Lobner, the COO, said on the earnings call:

“The one area of focus, and Dallas talked about this earlier, was the mom and pop shadow supply. We’re trying to keep an eye on that. Too early to tell where that’s going to go with interest rates where they are. You know, as we look more broadly though at the housing supply, it’s interesting.”

Where accidental landlords are most common

So where are accidental landlords most prevalent? Back in spring 2026, ResiClub analyzed a Zillow dataset covering 50 major metros, which measured the share of rental listings that had been listed for sale for at least two weeks, failed to sell, and were relisted as rentals within three months.

While that data is a little dated now, the directional finding remains: Accidental landlords are most common in the softer pockets of the U.S. housing market.

Major metros with the highest share of accidental landlord rental listings:

  • Denver: 4.9%
  • Houston: 4.2%
  • Austin: 4.1%
  • San Antonio : 3.9%
  • Portland, OR: 3.7%

Major metros with the lowest share of accidental landlord rental listings:

  • Boston: 0.6%
  • Providence, RI: 0.6%
  • New York: 0.7%
  • Hartford, CT: 0.7%
  • Buffalo: 0.8%

ResiClub’s spring 2026 analysis found a fairly strong negative relationship (R² = 0.58) between how much a metro’s home prices have shifted since their 2022 peak and its share of accidental landlords. Put simply: Markets with bigger price corrections, like Austin, Denver, and San Antonio, are more likely to see sellers pivot to renting rather than accept what they view as an unfavorable price cut. We also found a strong relationship (R² = 0.65) between accidental landlords and how far active inventory has rebounded above 2019 levels before the COVID-19 pandemic. More listings mean more competition, and more homes that fail to sell.

Why it matters for local markets

The concern for Invitation Homes is pricing power on new move-ins. In Q3 2026, the company’s renewing tenants paid 4.3% more than on their previous lease, while incoming tenants paid 0.2% less than the prior tenant in the same home.

The weakness on new leases was concentrated in Sun Belt markets where rental listing supply has been elevated: Phoenix (-2.9%), South Florida (-2.6%), Tampa, Florida, (-2.4%), Las Vegas (-2.3%), Atlanta (-0.7%), Houston (-0.5%), Denver (-0.4%), and Dallas (-0.1%). Many of those places also have higher shares of accidental landlords. If those accidental landlord shares rise further, it could undo some of the rental inventory cleanup that’s taken place in some of those markets over the past year.

In most markets, accidental landlording remains fairly niche. Many homeowners need the equity from selling their current home to buy their next one, which caps how many can hold onto a home and rent it out (especially given the current affordability picture). On the flip side, homeowners this cycle are under far less financial stress than during the financial crisis of 2008-09, and many locked in ultralow mortgage rates, which allows some to rent out a home at or above their monthly payment while they wait for the market to improve.

If economic conditions worsen, some of those accidental landlords could eventually become “capitulation sellers,” returning to the for-sale market at lower prices.

While shadow rental supply from accidental landlords is a headwind, Invitation Homes argues current rent vs. buy math is a tailwind. The giant SFR landlord says that as of September, it was on average more than $1,000 a month cheaper to lease a home than to own one in its markets.

OpenAI plans community agreements and infrastructure commitments as it prepares to rebrand data centers amid growing public opposition

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

OpenAI is reportedly preparing a major public relations campaign to influence how Americans view artificial intelligence, including a proposal to rename its data centers as “AI Compute Campuses,” Axios reports. The initiative comes ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections and forms a broader effort to influence the debate around AI before the 2028 presidential race. Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, noted that the midterms would be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028.” He expects AI to be a major issue for presidential candidates as the technology raises concerns over its impact on jobs, the economy, and the environment.

The proposed terminology change by OpenAI has been ongoing since August as the company focuses on promoting safeguards for the powerful technology, which Lehane described as “speed limits.” The proposed AI compute campuses is particularly interesting as it comes as opposition to large data centers accelerates across the U.S. Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity and water, with nearby communities raising concerns about noise, air pollution, rising utility bills and limited public consultation. OpenAI hopes to address these concerns through community agreements and a different way of presenting the infrastructure. “Compute campuses better describe the role of the infrastructure we are rebuilding for AI," a company spokesperson separately stated. He added that these projects represent long term investments in computing, energy infrastructure, and skilled jobs.

The latest proposal follows similar efforts by other technology companies to improve their relationship with communities hosting their infrastructure. In January, Microsoft announced a community-first approach, promising to cover electricity cost increases associated with its data centers, and invest in local infrastructure and jobs. However, while changing the name may be easier, changing public opinion may bring some headaches. A Redfin report in May found that 47% of Americans surveyed are opposed to having a new data center built in their community. Another report in August detailed how negotiations between developers and local authorities frequently take place behind non-disclosure agreements, leaving residents without access to important project information.

The resistance has also affected actual construction plans. At least 19 Michigan municipalities have already moved to restrict new data center developments after OpenAI and Oracle’s $16 billion Stargate project went ahead with their project in Sanile township despite local opposition. Meanwhile, Amazon abandoned plans for four data centers in northern Virginia last month following community pushback.

OpenAI is not alone in trying to reshape the language surrounding AI. President Donald Trump has previously pushed for terminology change, directing Federal agencies and urging AI companies to replace artificial intelligence with ‘super intelligence.’ Trump announced the change in late September arguing that the word "artificial" made the technology sound "fake." His administration subsequently instructed state department employees to use super intelligence or SI in official directives, websites, reports and policy documents.

Some technology executives have also embraced the terminology. Nvidia CEO Huang has previously referred to data centers as "superintelligence factories" while Elon musk announced plans to rename his AI company SpaceXAI to SpacexSI last month. Meta, meanwhile, established Meta superintelligence labs in 2025, and Microsoft has also assembled a team focused on developing superintelligence. OpenAI’s proposed terminology will now face a more difficult test than simply finding a name as communities will still want answers about the raised issues. Lehane, however, acknowledged that public scrutiny is part of the process saying, “Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects.”

#10524. How will the 2026 midterms impact the stock market? Experts warn of ‘uniquely difficult’ year, despite history of post-election rallies

Historically, midterms have been good for business in the months following the elections. Over the past 70 years, U.S. stocks, for the most part, have made gains in the months between midterm elections and the end of the year—and since 1980, the S&P 500 index has gone up 13.7% on average in the year after the midterm elections, according to a CNBC analysis.

But 2026 could be different. As things stand, it remains “uniquely difficult” to predict how this year’s midterms will affect the market, according to the Pew Research Center.

Here are a few reasons why.

Going into the midterms, the markets see uncertainty

If there’s one thing the markets do not like, it’s uncertainty—and on the eve of the 2026 midterm elections, there is plenty of it.

From the markets’ perspective, it remains unclear if or how the war in Iran will continue to raise already soaring oil prices; how inflation will play out—either with or without an interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve; and how the tech sector will fare amid growing concerns about runaway spending on artificial intelligence.

From a political perspective, the elections have the potential to redraw the political map, with a number of seats in play, including 435 in the U.S. House of Representatives and 35 in the U.S. Senate.

There are also 36 state governorships, thousands of state legislative seats, and 145 state ballot measures that will be decided, according to the Taubman Center for American Politics and Policy at Brown’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.

“The 2026 election is among the most consequential in decades,” said Eric Patashnik, a political science professor and director of the Taubman Center. “Understanding how the U.S. political system works—and why our governing institutions are struggling to solve the problems Americans care about—has never been more urgent.”

With a number of races too close to call, it remains to be seen whether the Democrats will take back control of the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, and how the markets will react.

Could there be a rally? Or could we see stock drops in government-connected sectors such as defense, healthcare, cryptocurrency, and AI—as a Democratic sweep in one or both branches of Congress could empower the party to investigate U.S. companies? Even for experts, it’s impossible to predict.

#10523. What Is the Best UI Testing Tool? 8 Tools Compared by the Job They Do (2026)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The ideal UI testing tool is the one that discovers what your users discover first: broken layouts, usability issues that no longer work, and new accessibility issues in all the browsers your users use before a change goes into the repository. In 2026, most frontend teams don't rely on a single tool to do all of that. The best setups involve two layers: a test runner layer that launches the browser and monitors behavior, and a UI testing and review platform that visually checks the outcome and routes changes to the right stakeholders for sign-off.

Even with the right stack, it still relies on what your team needs to catch. Different teams will focus on different points: a QA team trying to automate checkout flows, a design system team defending shared components, and a single developer working on a tight budget will all be somewhere different. This guide is categorized by the job these UI testing tools do, then connects them.

Most "best UI testing tool" lists rank test runners and visual testing platforms against each other as if they were interchangeable. They aren't. UI testing covers four distinct jobs:

Functional testing: Does the UI respond correctly when a user clicks, types, or hovers?

Visual testing: Does the UI still look right across layout, color, typography, and spacing?

Accessibility testing: Can people using keyboards and screen readers use it, and did this change introduce new violations?

Cross-browser and device coverage: Does it work in Safari on mobile, not just Chrome on a developer's laptop?

There are also other levels of UI tests. Unit tests test the logic but don't interact with the UI. End-to-end (E2E) tests represent the full user journey in a browser but are difficult to set up, hard to troubleshoot when the bug is a visual detail, and can't practically test every state. Between the extremes of unit tests and E2E tests, component tests simulate each component's behavior in a real browser using fixed inputs, offering speed closer to unit tests and user-level coverage closer to E2E. Many teams maintain a thin layer of E2E tests for critical journeys, and they have component tests for the dozens of states a component may be in.

These tools are organized by job so you can stack them rather than choose one winner.

Prices are taken from each vendor's site or published comparisons as of October 2026. Check current pricing before you buy.

These platforms sit on top of your test runner. They capture rendered UI, compare it to approved baselines, and give your team a place to review what changed.

Chromatic is a UI testing and review platform made by the Storybook team. It catches visual, interaction, and accessibility bugs in components and pages before they merge, and it gives developers, designers, and product managers one place to review UI changes and sign off. Chromatic's team is the core maintainer of Storybook, which has about 90,000 GitHub stars and 17 million weekly npm downloads, and a Vitest core maintainer on the team built Chromatic's Vitest integration. Chromatic is used by 45 Fortune 100 companies, including GitHub, Shopify, Microsoft, Adobe, the BBC, and monday.com

Pricing: Free plan with 5,000 snapshots per month (Chrome only), unlimited projects and users. Starter is $179/month for 35,000 snapshots and adds Safari, Firefox, and Edge. Pro is $399/month for 85,000 snapshots. Enterprise is custom, with SSO, SCIM, SLA support, and data retention. TurboSnap snapshots count as 0.2 of a regular snapshot.

Trade-offs: Chromatic is strongest when your UI is built from components. Teams with no component tests can start from Playwright or Cypress E2E tests, but they'll get the most value once components are covered too. Snapshot usage also grows with each browser and viewport you add, so plan coverage before you scale it.

Best for: Design system teams, product teams that want designers and PMs to approve UI changes, React Native teams, and Vitest-first teams that want visual testing without baselines stored in the repo.

Percy is BrowserStack's visual testing platform. It captures screenshots from your existing tests, renders them across browsers and responsive widths, and highlights pixel differences for review.

Strengths: Framework-agnostic SDKs for Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, and Storybook. App Percy covers native mobile apps. The free plan includes 5,000 screenshots per month with unlimited users and projects.

Trade-offs: Percy is page-oriented, and each page rendered in each browser at each width counts as a separate screenshot, so usage climbs quickly with cross-browser coverage. Percy compares feature branches against a base branch, which teams with complex branching should test early. Reviewers see rendered screenshots rather than an inspectable copy of the code under test, so debugging a diff usually means reproducing it locally.

Pricing: Free tier, then paid plans with fixed screenshot allowances and overage.

Best for: Teams already paying for BrowserStack that want visual checks on page-level E2E tests.

Applitools Eyes uses Visual AI to compare screenshots the way a person would, with match levels that can ignore content changes and focus on layout. Its Ultrafast Grid re-renders captured page states across many browser, viewport, and device combinations.

Strengths: Mature AI matching, broad browser and device coverage, Figma and Storybook testing, accessibility testing, and an MCP server. Higher tiers add AI-driven functional testing and plain-English test authoring.

Trade-offs: Applitools is priced and packaged for enterprises. There's a free trial but no free plan, and the Starter plan is $667/month billed annually for 100,000 component checkpoints or 1,000 page checkpoints. Professional and Enterprise are custom-priced.

Best for: Large QA organizations with big cross-browser matrices and budget for a dedicated visual AI platform.

Argos is an open source visual testing platform with SDKs for Playwright, Storybook, Vitest, and Cypress. It adds cloud baselines and team review on top of the screenshots your tests already produce.

Strengths: Simple flat pricing. The Hobby plan includes 5,000 screenshots per month, and Pro is $100/month for 35,000 screenshots, with a budget cap available.

Trade-offs: Argos focuses on visual diffs. Argos compares screenshots captured by your own test runs, so browser coverage depends on what your CI runs, and it doesn't offer hosted mobile simulators. It also has a smaller ecosystem than the larger platforms.

Best for: Small teams that want hosted visual review at a predictable price.

Test runners click, type, and assert. They're free and open source, and every platform above builds on them. On their own, they offer limited visual testing: built-in screenshot assertions store baselines in your repository, rendering can drift between laptops and CI, and designers have no review interface.

Playwright is Microsoft's open-source browser automation framework. It runs tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, with auto-waiting, trace viewer debugging and code generation, and supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.

Visual testing: Playwright's toHaveScreenshot assertion compares screenshots against baselines stored in Git. It works, but baselines must be regenerated per operating system, and accepting a change means rerunning with an update flag.

Best for: Teams automating critical user journeys such as sign-up, checkout and login. Pair it with a platform like Chromatic for visual review across real browsers.

Cypress is an open-source testing tool that runs inside the browser, with time-travel debugging that shows the app at each step of a test. It supports both E2E and component testing.

Visual testing: Cypress has no built-in visual comparison and relies on plugins or a platform such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools. Cypress Cloud, its paid service, adds recording, parallelization, flake detection and add-ons for accessibility and UI coverage.

Best for: Frontend developers who want fast feedback and an interactive test runner while they build.

Storybook is the open source workshop for building UI components in isolation. Each story captures one component state, and those stories double as test cases.

Testing features: Interaction tests with play functions and Testing Library, accessibility checks with the a11y addon, and a Vitest integration that runs stories as component tests.

Visual testing: Storybook doesn't diff screenshots on its own. Chromatic, built by the same team, is its visual testing and review layer.

Best for: Design system and component library teams, and any team practicing component-driven development.

Vitest Browser Mode runs component tests in a real browser instead of a simulated DOM, using Playwright or WebdriverIO under the hood.

Visual testing: Vitest's toMatchScreenshot assertion stores screenshots in the repository. For large projects, this can bloat the repo and baselines drift between machines. Chromatic can take Vitest Browser Mode tests with no code changes and run them in a stable cloud environment instead.

Best for: Teams already writing Vitest tests who want them to check how the UI looks without adopting a new framework.

Start from the problem your team is trying to fix:

"Shared component changes keep breaking other teams' screens." Test at the component level with Storybook or Vitest Browser Mode and Chromatic, so the change shows up on the pull request that caused it.

"Our Playwright tests pass, but the layout still breaks in Safari." Functional assertions don't check appearance. Add a visual testing platform that renders in Safari, such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools.

"We turned off screenshot tests because of false alarms." Look for deterministic component states and flake controls such as Chromatic's SteadySnap, or AI matching such as Applitools.

"Designers find UI bugs after release." Choose a platform with a review and approval workflow, and make sign-off a required pull request check.

"AI coding agents keep inventing components." Give agents access to your real component library, for example through Chromatic's hosted MCP, and run every agent-built change through the same UI tests as human code.

"We have no budget." Use Playwright or Vitest screenshot assertions, or start on the free tiers of Chromatic, Percy or Argos.

A practical, well-covered setup for a React web app looks like this:

Unit tests in Vitest for logic and utilities.

Storybook stories or Vitest Browser Mode tests for every meaningful component state, with interaction tests on key components.

Chromatic running visual, interaction and accessibility tests on those components in Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge on every pull request, with designers assigned as reviewers.

A thin layer of Playwright E2E tests for sign-up, checkout and other critical journeys, also captured in Chromatic so page-level visual changes go through the same review.

This keeps most UI coverage in fast, deterministic component tests, while E2E tests confirm the journeys that matter most still work end to end.

Playwright is the best free tool for E2E UI testing, and Storybook is the best free tool for testing component states. For visual testing, Chromatic, Percy and Argos all offer free tiers of around 5,000 snapshots or screenshots per month.

UI testing is the broad practice of checking that an interface works for users, including functional, visual and accessibility checks. Visual testing is one part of it: comparing rendered UI against approved baselines to catch unintended changes in layout, color, typography and spacing.

No. Chromatic was built by the Storybook team, but it also runs visual tests from Vitest Browser Mode, Playwright and Cypress tests, and from React Native Storybook on iOS and Android simulators.

Playwright's toHaveScreenshot covers basic visual checks, but baselines live in your repo, rendering can differ between machines, and there's no review interface for designers. Teams with several reviewers or many browsers usually add a platform on top.

Most teams use both. Component tests cover individual UI states quickly and reliably, while a smaller set of E2E tests confirms that critical user journeys work across the whole app.

#10520. The midterms’ biggest branding trend? Centrism

When Griffin Glaze, a graphic designer, got the job to design James Talarico’s campaign branding, she had just 10 days to do it. Talarico, a Texan who is running for a seat in the U.S. Senate, wanted something that looked unique and nonpartisan.

“A lot of what they were looking for was something that felt different,” Glaze tells Fast Company. The North Carolina designer came up with a visual identity inspired by hand-painted signage at Baptist churches, with texture and imperfection designed into its typography and asterisks for decorative Texas stars. Though they tried out different color palettes, they kept coming back to black and white because it didn’t feel linked to a political party.

“I think for him, it was really about finding something that could be healing, more of a bridge builder, that when people saw it, they weren’t immediately jumping to a specific party,” Glaze says.

Talarico (full disclosure: he’s a Democrat) isn’t alone.

Across the midterm campaign, candidates have branded themselves to play down their party affiliation, and for good reason. Gallup polling earlier this year found 45% of U.S. adults self-identify as independent, a record high. In an environment where both major parties and the president are unpopular, candidates would rather not be associated with any of it, and it’s showing up visually in their logos, mailers, and advertisements.

For candidates actually running as independents, the trend towards less partisan branding means designing the word “independent” directly into their logos. But Democrats and Republicans too have found ways to signal a break from their parties.

In the race for Iowa governor, neither campaign website mentions their party or President Donald Trump, and both candidates use green as their campaign color with logos designed to represent unity. The logo of Zach Lahn, a Republican, says “Iowa First,” while that of the Democrat, Rob Sand, shows shaking hands, above the tagline “Governor for All.”

In Arizona, Governor Katie Hobbs, a Democrat, uses a circular logo with the tagline “For Arizona.” Her state party organization sent mailers to unaffiliated voters that play up elements of her record that would appeal to both sides, like public safety, slashing red tape (for conservatives), and expanding the state’s school lunch program and canceling medical debt (for liberals).

Tropes that were once associated with Republicans have gone bipartisan this year. Democrats are using their own versions of logos like Trump’s, inspired by the so-called “MAGA box,” or adapting his “America First” slogan for their own states to communicate that they’ll put their state ahead of party.

Scott Sutton, president and CEO of the New Jersey print shop Burlington Press, says that while most of the design and print work he’s gotten this year has been extremely partisan, it often comes in the form of attacking the other side for being too extreme.

“We’ve had several Republicans reference socialism to attack their opponents, and equally harsh criticism from Democrats against MAGA,” Sutton says. Even in their attacks, candidates are moving towards the center.

Candidates who play up their bipartisan appeal are trying to inoculate themselves from attacks like this. To show how centrist he would be in office, Adam Hamilton, a Kansas pastor and U.S. Senate candidate, stands in the middle of the field in his 30-second spot “Smack Dab in the Middle” and says, “Here in Kansas, we’re smack dab in the middle of the country” as a metaphor for moderation.

“We’re proud of being in the middle politically too, and that puts us about a million miles away from the extreme politics of Washington that are tearing us apart and driving up prices,” he says, but at no point does he mention he’s a Democrat. The closing tagline of the ad is “Time for Something Different.”

Among advertising for Republican House and Senate candidates, mentions of bipartisanship, working across the aisle, or “both sides” are up 60% from 2024, according to data from the ad tracking firm AdImpact. Mentions of Trump are way down as Republicans seek to distance themselves from him and his agenda.

Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for a U.S. Senate seat from Michigan, practically sounds like a Democrat in a recent ad. It shows him seated in bar with a Canadian beer in front of him, saying, “Canada is not our enemy” and that if elected, he’ll “end this tariff war. Now.” Zach Nunn, an Iowa Republican running for reelection in a House district the nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates as “Lean Democratic,” touts his ranking as one of the three most bipartisan members of Congress as a selling point in his ad “Iowa Comes First.”

Nearly six in 10 Americans have unfavorable views of the Democratic and Republican parties, according to Pew Research Center. Candidates branding themselves to stand apart from them this year are just taking their cues from voters.

#10518. Major League Baseball’s new look pays homage to the sport’s history

Major League Baseball has a new look, courtesy of an all-star lineup of type designers.

In 2020, after MLB moved to its new headquarters in New York City, it reached out to Mother Design, the branding and design agency behind work for brands like Cadillac, Tripadvisor, and the scented water bottle Air Up. The league was looking to expand professional baseball’s fandom and talent, and it wanted its visual identity to feel unified.

Beginning in late 2022, Mother Design started building out MLB’s new brand architecture, which was introduced beginning in 2024 on a rolling basis. The league’s famous silhouetted batter logo, designed in 1968 by Jerry Dior, was left untouched, but MLB’s wordmark was updated to fit into larger visual system that’s now complete.

As part of the multiyear brand refresh, the agency tapped five type designers or foundries chosen for their individual specialties to build out a one-of-a-kind font book that shows up across the league, from its Ballpark app and venues to social channels and special events.

Each font in the brand—MLB Franklin, MLB Clarendon, MLB Flare, MLB Block, and MLB Script—was chosen because it’s a style that was present in baseball in the early 20th century in some form or another.

“It’s ensuring that we’ve got these visual cues and these letterforms that have been part of our visual vernacular for longer than any of us have been alive,” Mark Sloan, Mother Design’s New York City head of design, tells Fast Company. “How do we make sure that we carry that forward and we honor that tradition, but that we build them in a way that is prepared for retina screens [on smartphones] and extremely small spaces as well as emphatic, large moments. That’s really the crux of it.”

The typographers for the project were purposefully enlisted. MLB Script was designed by the Bay Area foundry OH no Type Co., which was selected for its attention to unexpected quirky details. The variable typeface includes flags, the horizontal stripe from a word’s final letter that underlines the word and looks quintessentially baseball.

MLB Flare has a handlettering style designed by the Uruguayan foundry Tipotype. The aim is to feel warm and charming, and to reflect and honor the cultural connection between baseball and Latin America.

“There is a long tradition of Latin American players in MLB, so the Latin influence is naturally part of the game,” Tipotype’s cofounders, Martín Sommaruga and Vicente Lamónaca, say in an email. “The Latin community also has a strong presence not as a distinctive feature, but as a fundamental part of the sport itself.”

The type designer Nick Sherman designed a customized version of MLB Franklin, a classic American grotesque-sans serif used on scoreboards that could be seen in stadiums during the recent World Series. MLB Clarendon is similarly a customized version of a classic slab-serif font found throughout baseball history, to which the type designer David Jonathan Ross gave added flexibility in weights and widths.

Skye Dillon, a type designer who specializes in sports branding and designed the 2026 MLB All-Star Game style guide, designed the octagonal MLB Block. It’s based on letterform found on jersey names and numerals and lettering at venues like Ebbets Field, the now-vanished ballpark where the Dodgers played when they were based in Brooklyn.

Research for the brand refresh included books, baseball cards, ticket stubs, felt letters, and individual clubs’ venues, history, and ephemera. The goal was to find visual through lines that go back the furthest but still feel relevant, as if they were designed today, says Sloan, Mother Design’s head of design.

Baseball is rich with typographic inspiration, from jersey lettering and numerals to logos like the interlocking NY monograms for the Yankees and Mets. Sloan compared baseball to “a visual history of the country itself,” and says it’s arguably responsible for keeping a lot of typographic styles alive and relevant in pop culture.

“If you look at something like baseball script, for example, it’s something that as Americans, it’s in our visual consciousness,” Sloan says. “It sort of comes in and out of fashion in the world of branding, but it’s always been in fashion in baseball.”

#10517. Motorola is filling the gap OnePlus left behind, mostly

As we near the launch of Motorola’s return to the flagship space, it’s becoming clear that the company is ready to fill a gap left by the departure of OnePlus, though there’s one very obvious difference between the two.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

The Motorola Signature 27’s launch is coming up fast and, with it, the first truly exciting flagship the company has launched widely in quite some time. There have been a handful of high-end Moto devices in recent years, but this is the first one in quite a while where it seems Motorola is holding nothing back.

Between a powerful Snapdragon chip, top-tier cameras, and rumors of a massive battery, this is shaping up to be something special. Of course, all-out flagships like this aren’t uncommon in some parts of the world. Oppo, Honor, and other Chinese brands have been building devices like this for years but, especially in the US, they’re just completely lacking, especially now that OnePlus is dead. While OnePlus flagships in more recent years have not quite risen to the same bar as Oppo’s, they’ve been the best equivalent in the States and, now, they’re just gone.

Motorola is stepping up in a big way here, and seems to be the closest many are going to get to a OnePlus replacement.

It’s fitting, really. As much as I’d love to have Google Pixel step up its game here, Motorola’s Lenovo backing and long history in the smartphone space more than earns its spot as a proper flagship smartphone maker. The problem, really, is just going to boil down to pricing.

OnePlus was well known for top-tier specs, of course, but it built its brand on doing so at a lower price point. Even in its final days where prices were creeping higher than ever, a OnePlus flagship was still priced equal to or less than most competitors. Motorola Signature 27 does not seem to be trying to recover that part of OnePlus’ reputation based on early pricing leaks. RAMageddon surely isn’t helping matters, but Motorola’s return to the flagship space is not going to come cheap from the sound of it.

Another sore point for Motorola is in software updates, but it’s not like OnePlus was really doing that well in that regard anyway. Things are moving in a better direction with Motorola moving up to 7-year commitments on certain devices, but there’s still room for improvement and quite the poor track record to make up for.

With the launch of Motorola Signature 27 mere weeks away, I’m personally very excited to see what the company has in store. What do you think?

While the scale of the problem remains unclear, Apple’s iPhone Duo is cracking for many in the same place, suggesting there’s a manufacturing problem in play. It’s not quite an OG Galaxy Fold debacle, but it doesn’t feel far off either.

Google’s latest frontier AI model has been announced in Gemini 4 Carbon. The company says it makes major leaps forward for coding and other purposes and outranks the competition but, like Argon, it’s not immediately available.

After being announced earlier this month, we reviewed the Fitbit Edge this week and the tracker is also now on sale. While it feels like an awkward middle child between the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, owners of prior Charge trackers will likely appreciate the upgrades it brings to the table.

Amazon’s closure email cites a verification process and offers no reason.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI creator Nick Saraev says on X that Amazon closed his account after he tried to buy seven Nvidia DGX Spark AI mini-PCs. The closure email cites a verification process and gives no reason. Epic CEO Tim Sweeney chimed in that his regular orders would go through, then get canceled before arrival, after he tried to buy two GPUs.

Update: Amazon just closed my account.Buying even modest amounts of compute immediately puts you on a watchlist. Be careful!November 1, 2026

Saraev puts it plainly that “Amazon just closed my account” and that “Buying even modest amounts of compute immediately puts you on a watchlist.” He was “4 orders deep,” and Amazon will no longer allow him to buy DGX Sparks.

The shared screenshots indicate those orders were all canceled, with each stating, “Your order was canceled. You have not been charged for this order.” Although he does not give a unit count, the screenshots indicate he tried to buy seven DGX Sparks in total. All show the same listing, with 128GB of memory and 4TB of storage.

Amazon’s support account did respond to his earlier post, about three hours before his closure post, offering a review. The shared email shows that Amazon had “made the final decision” to close his account after review; no reason was given. However, it did mention “previous attempts to verify your account,” and he says he did go through the verification process, but seven DGX Sparks is a significant amount that might draw suspicion. Either way, Amazon’s Conditions of Use reserve the right to “refuse service, terminate accounts” or “cancel orders in its sole discretion.”

He’s not alone in running into trouble with the company. Sweeney says that “Amazon didn’t cancel my account but continued accepting all my regular orders and canceling them just prior to arrival dates, after I tried to buy two NVIDIA GPUs. Rather bizarre.” Nvidia GPUs are often used for local inference. Saraev replied that everyone would “appreciate a bit more transparency.”

Also, in September, Dracones89 on the Nvidia developer forum shared that one Amazon account was hit with “suspicious activity locks” while trying to buy a pair of Asus GX10s; the user ended up with two DGX Sparks from Micro Center instead. Another X user, @PurzBeats, wrote, “They canceled the order when I tried to buy my 5090, twice.” This is a different trajectory than the OpenClaw days of Mac minis, when buyers faced long delivery waits rather than canceled orders or closed accounts.

With local inference remaining of high interest to many, particularly AI influencers, the event is potentially disturbing, especially after recent comments about self-owned DRAM by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. While this time it was a guy who helps entrepreneurs and small businesses implement AI and claims 500K on YouTube and 700K on Instagram, the slope is slippery, although Saraev’s orders are hardly typical.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The 128GB DGX Spark has an MSRP of $6,950, but it may be found at 20% or more over that: two Amazon listings showed $8,499.99 and $9,499.99 when we checked today, which would put seven at roughly $59,500 to $66,500. Both showed Prime delivery tomorrow, so the hardware is still on sale there.

Hardware has been climbing in price, largely due to rising memory costs. As open-weight models have become more popular, so has local AI inference. The combination may make retailers uneasy, as you’re dealing with high ticket prices and there has been uncertainty about the safety of models as they have improved, with open-source AI agent tools reportedly being used in multiple recent cybersecurity incidents.

Micro Center, a different retailer, required one buyer to sign an Advanced Computing Product Purchaser Declaration with photo ID, end user, and an install location, just for a workstation with an RTX 5090. This form specifically forbade exporting or reselling the hardware, which might give a little insight into Amazon’s reasoning, too. Amazon’s conditions also say customers “must comply with all U.S. or other export and re-export restrictions.” China and the U.S. remain locked in a fight over exports of AI hardware.

Amazon hasn’t explained itself, but the attention this is getting may motivate a more detailed response. Right now, it’s a warning signal to users looking to buy significant amounts of hardware for AI work, at least from traditional online retailers. Brick-and-mortar stores, like Micro Center, may crack down further to prevent workarounds designed to export the hardware illegally.

#10514. Personality is the new fuel for marketing

Through the annals of advertising history, the gospel of brand building has been written around a single capital letter: P.

The classical four P’s of price, product, place, and promotion were drilled into marketing minds in college. The major brand totem, P for positioning, is where companies spent millions defining razor-thin functional benefits, establishing category ladders, and staking claim to owned territory in the consumer’s mind. The last decade’s reverence has been for the all-guiding P for purpose, where brands raced to solve global crises, writing manifesto after manifesto, making very similar-looking ads to save the world (and sell products).

Now, the pendulum has swung again. While some would argue that positioning could feel cold and analytical, and purpose maybe grew lofty and detached, the new imperative for business growth is infinitely more human. This might arguably be at a time when consumers want something more human and real.

ENTER THE ERA OF PERSONALITY.

Personality is the new fuel for supercharging commercial growth. It is no longer enough for a brand to stand for an ideal or a functional benefit; it has to show up as a living, breathing entity with a voice, a soul, a vibe, and a belief system. Needing a distinct perspective on the world and attitude that consumers can feel part of, co-create with, and ultimately believe in, is key.

Adzooma research suggests that 57.5% of consumers buy brands with strong, distinct personalities. Meanwhile, according to the Future Proof report from The Daily Aus, only one in five feel positively about a brand when it relies solely on describing itself as “purpose-driven.” With information overload in this attention economy, and perhaps if we dare say it, as a small rally against AI, we are seeing consumers gravitating towards brands that make them feel something real. And this shift is creating commercial velocity for those brands that are determining how to win in this moment.

Duolingo transformed its green owl mascot from a simple app icon into a slightly unhinged, self-aware cultural icon with a living and breathing point of view in the world. It scaled fandom, deep commercial impact, and drove 1.7 billion views.

And e.l.f. Beauty delivered 30 consecutive quarters of business growth by being a bold disrupter with a kind heart. Its product and personality ecosystem goes hand in hand, allowing its community to feel, live, and be the DNA of its brand. 

Poppi unleashed a personality that shaped a new category with a distinctive and fresh POV, provoking a $1.95 billion acquisition by Pepsi while getting over 1 billion views on TikTok on the journey.

Liquid Death, one could argue, was the early creator of this movement. It brought personality to water with a living content machine that unleashed who they were in the world, stimulating a 6-year CAGR of 122% since its 2019 launch.

So how do brands develop a new weapon beyond expected corporate tone guidelines and build a personality and world that is rich, deep, and drives growth?

It starts by rethinking how personality operates.

4 PILLARS OF BRAND PERSONALITY

To build a personality that flexes and wins across a community-led world, brands must become the masters of four fundamentals:

1. How you speak (voice and fluidity): Stop trapping your brand inside rigid, 50-page tonal guidelines. In a fast-moving culture, your voice needs to flex. It’s about codifying the rhythms and rules of how your brand talks so that it retains unmistakable recognition whether responding in a social media comment or running a Super Bowl ad.

2. How you look (visual identity): We live in a visually driven culture where brand lust is dictated by design. Craft a signature look, and be clear on your distinctive brand assets, but be fluid with it. You can play and flex how you show up for different audiences while still always looking and feeling like yourself.

3. How you feel (vibe and energy): Define the energy your brand brings to the room. Brands that possess a clear “vibe” can react, improvise, and play in real time alongside their communities, and become magnetic to the consumers they want to attract.

4. How you act (real-world behavior): Personality is proven through action, not empty claims. When a brand uses its core belief system to do bold, unexpected things in the real world, it turns passive consumers into passionate advocates. This is where personality breathes life back into purpose.

    BE A CATALYST

    If you can unlock the awesomeness of your brand, the final shift you need to make is changing how you behave as a brand leader. Unleash a new personality within yourself.

    For decades, marketing leadership was defined by brand guardianship. Leaders were trained to protect the brand identity, enforce rigid guidelines, and shield the company from risk.

    But in a world driven by fast-moving communities, creator economies, and real-time culture, protection is passive. Guardians end up building polished, potentially lifeless museum artifacts that can trigger a brand’s demise.

    To succeed today, leaders must shift from being guardians to being catalysts.

    A catalyst doesn’t lock the brand in a vault. A catalyst ignites the brand’s personality, empowering teams and communities to play with it, flex it, and bring energy, empathy, and humanity to everything it touches. They live, breathe, and become the brand.

    So stop playing it safe, be comfortable in the chaos, and embrace the fluidity of what can help you win. Find your authentic voice. Rise above the sea of sameness. Unleash uniqueness. Let your brand’s personality lead the way to fuel your next phase of growth.

    Chris Kay is the international CEO of 72andSunny.

    #10511. Election Day is unfolding across America after a surge in early voting for the midterms

    The final day of voting in this year’s midterm elections arrived Tuesday against a backdrop of uncertainty after a year in which President Donald Trump has tried to interfere in how states run their elections and sown doubts about the outcome should Republicans lose.

    Millions of Americans already have cast their ballots, with early voting turnout on pace to eclipse that of the last midterm elections. In contrast to the president’s continued rhetoric about election cheating, voting so far has unfolded with relatively few problems.

    Trump has spent months trying to use the power of the presidency to put his thumb on the scale of this year’s elections, which will determine whether his party keeps control of Congress.

    His Justice and Homeland Security departments have been involved in a massive hunt for voters who are not U.S. citizens, at one point engaging in a made-for-the-cameras predawn operation that led to more than two dozen arrests in California. The Department of Justice was planning its largest-ever effort to monitor Election Day polling places, countered by an even larger effort among Democrats and allied groups, and at the president’s urging had sued to block certification of Alaska’s results if the outcome of the Senate race favored Democrats.

    At the same time, Trump’s constant false claims about widespread voter fraud led election officials and Democratic groups across the country to plan for the possibility of immigration agents at voting sites or federal officers seizing voting machines. His administration has insisted that no armed federal officials would be guarding the polls on Election Day.

    Courts have blocked the Trump administration’s efforts to influence elections

    In the run-up to Tuesday, none of the steps Democrats most feared had come to pass, and the Republican administration’s legal maneuvers had been largely blocked by the courts.

    One of the Trump administration’s most high-profile attempts to interfere in state elections was turned away Monday night by the U.S. Supreme Court, which rejected its push to force California to set aside thousands of ballots as part of its search for noncitizen voters. In another Monday night ruling, a federal judge said the Trump administration must stop sending voter lists of alleged noncitizens to election officials.

    Even the administration’s own record of arrests and charges has demonstrated what research and state investigations have made clear for years — that instances of noncitizens casting ballots are extremely rare.

    Monday’s rulings followed another defeat for the president at the Supreme Court less than two months ago, when it rejected his attempt to limit mail balloting through changes at the Postal Service. That directive was included in one of two executive orders Trump has signed during his second term that attempted to federalize certain aspects of elections, even though the Constitution gives the states, and sometimes Congress, the authority to set election rules.

    Voting begins smoothly with some weather disruptions in the Southwest

    The first polling sites opened at 6 a.m. EST Tuesday in a handful of states — Connecticut, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Missouri, New Jersey, New York and Virginia.

    Heavy rains and flash flooding in a swath of the Southwest were expected to make it harder for some voters to reach polling places in parts of Colorado, Arizona, Utah and New Mexico. Election administrators in the Navajo Nation announced changes to several of its polling locations, and in Utah’s rural San Juan County, voters were being allowed to vote electronically on Tuesday because some of them may not be able to reach polling places.

    Election administrators and voting rights advocates have been advising voters casting late absentee ballots to use drop boxes or deliver them to polling places in person rather than mail them. The advice came after concerns emerged that recent changes in U.S. Postal Service operations could result in postmarking delays that would mean mail ballots could not be counted. Late-arriving ballots or late postmarks disenfranchised tens of thousands of voters in California, Oregon and Washington, which mail ballots to all voters, during this year’s primaries.

    Trump hasn’t committed to accepting the election results

    The most significant disruptions ahead of Election Day were the Trump administration’s attempts to interfere. Voting rights groups, Democrats and the Justice Department have been exchanging a flurry of legal filings over alleged noncitizen voters, federal election monitors, federal intimidation of election officials and other concerns. They reveal how Trump’s attempts to expand federal control over state-run elections — combined with high-stakes races — are resulting in court battles that could extend past Election Day into ballot counting and certification of the results.

    Election law experts said Trump’s lawsuits go beyond historic norms, but they said the administration’s legal arguments were unlikely to convince the courts.

    Trump also has ramped up his own equivocations about whether the election will be legitimate, as he has in the past. A week before Election Day, when a reporter asked him if he would accept the results, he offered a qualified answer.

    “I will if they are honest,” he said.

    Associated Press writer Geoff Mulvihill contributed to this report.

    —Ali Swenson, Associated Press

    #10510. Generating Web-Ready Images With AI: Formats, Sizes, and srcset Done Right

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    AI-generated images are becoming an important part of modern web development. Developers use them for website banners, product visuals, blog illustrations, backgrounds, and other digital content. However, creating an image is only the first step. Preparing it for efficient web delivery is equally important.

    Unoptimized images can increase page size, consume unnecessary bandwidth, and delay page rendering. These problems can affect Core Web Vitals, especially Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), which measures how quickly the largest visible content element appears.

    This guide explains how to optimize AI-generated images using practical techniques, including image resizing, modern formats, Node.js automation, responsive delivery, and performance testing.

    Images often represent a significant portion of a webpage's total download size. When developers upload large images without processing them, visitors may experience slower loading times, particularly on mobile networks.

    Large image files that take longer to download.

    Incorrect dimensions for different screen sizes.

    Missing image dimensions that cause layout shifts.

    Excessive compression that reduces visual quality.

    Unnecessary downloads caused by poor responsive configuration.

    A consistent optimization workflow helps address these problems while maintaining the intended visual appearance.

    Before preparing an image, determine where it will appear on the website. A full-width hero banner requires different dimensions from a product thumbnail or a small article illustration.

    These are suggested dimensions, not fixed requirements. The actual size depends on the website layout and the devices being supported.

    When preparing source visuals, developers can compare different AI image tools to understand how image generation workflows handle aspect ratios, output dimensions, and visual details.

    Regardless of the generation method, keep an original high-quality version. This master file can be used to create smaller versions without repeatedly compressing an already optimized image.

    Choosing an appropriate image format can reduce file size while maintaining acceptable visual quality.

    AVIF: Provides efficient compression for many photographs and detailed illustrations.

    WebP: Supports lossy and lossless compression, transparency, and animation.

    JPEG: Remains useful for photographs and environments requiring broad compatibility.

    PNG: Suitable for screenshots, lossless graphics, and images that require transparency.

    No format is automatically the best choice for every image. Developers should compare the resulting file sizes and inspect image quality before selecting a format.

    For technical details, consult the MDN Web Docs guide to image file formats.

    Manually resizing multiple images can become time-consuming. Automation provides a consistent way to generate different image dimensions and formats.

    Sharp is a Node.js library that supports resizing, compression, and image conversion.

    The script generates WebP and AVIF versions at several widths.

    For additional configuration options, refer to the official Sharp documentation.

    Responsive image delivery allows browsers to select an appropriate image based on available resources and screen layout.

    The HTML srcset attribute provides multiple image candidates, while sizes describes the expected rendered width.

    The browser uses the available image candidates and layout information to select a suitable resource.

    Make sure the sizes attribute accurately reflects the actual website layout. Incorrect values can cause browsers to download larger images than necessary.

    Responsive delivery is particularly useful when the same visual appears in different layouts across desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.

    The HTML picture element allows developers to provide alternative image formats with a fallback.

    The browser selects a supported source, while the img element provides fallback behavior and alternative text.

    Always verify that the referenced files exist and that their dimensions match the intended layout.

    Images without defined dimensions can cause page content to move while resources are loading. This can negatively affect Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

    Include width and height attributes whenever possible:

    The browser can use the dimensions to reserve the appropriate space before the image finishes loading.

    Images below the initial viewport can also use native lazy loading:

    However, avoid lazy-loading the main hero image when it contributes to LCP. Important above-the-fold images should be loaded promptly.

    Reducing file size should not significantly affect the visual details required by the website.

    This is particularly important for images containing:

    A practical quality-checking process includes:

    Compare the optimized image with its original version.

    Inspect the image at its actual display dimensions.

    Test the output on mobile and desktop screens.

    The smallest file is not necessarily the best option. A slightly larger image may provide noticeably better visual quality.

    After implementing the optimization workflow, test the actual website rather than relying only on exported file sizes.

    Open Chrome DevTools and select the Network panel. Filter requests by images and reload the webpage.

    Mobile devices receive appropriately sized images.

    The browser downloads unnecessary image files.

    Modern formats are being served correctly.

    Important images load without unnecessary delays.

    Image dimensions match their display requirements.

    You can inspect the image source selected by the browser using:

    For websites containing multiple images, inspect each relevant element.

    Finally, run an audit using Google PageSpeed Insights. It can help identify oversized images and other performance issues.

    The web.dev guide to optimizing LCP also provides useful technical guidance for diagnosing loading delays.

    Remember that image optimization is only one part of website performance. Server response times, caching, CSS, and JavaScript execution can also influence page loading.

    Uploading original images without checking their dimensions.

    Assuming one image format always provides the best compression.

    Using incorrect responsive image settings.

    Lazy-loading important above-the-fold images.

    Ignoring the actual image selected by the browser.

    Measuring file size without checking visual quality.

    A proper testing process helps identify these issues before they affect visitors.

    No. AVIF often provides efficient compression, but results depend on image content, encoding settings, and quality requirements. Comparing both formats is the best approach.

    Four to six sizes may be sufficient for many websites. The ideal number depends on the layout, responsive breakpoints, and supported devices.

    Yes. Reducing the size of the main content image, providing responsive versions, and avoiding unnecessary loading delays can improve LCP when that image is the largest contentful element.

    No. Lazy loading is useful for images outside the initial viewport. Important images near the top of a webpage should generally load promptly.

    The fundamental optimization techniques are the same as those used for conventional images. However, generated visuals may contain complex textures and fine details that require careful inspection after compression.

    AI-generated images can improve website design, but efficient delivery requires more than simply exporting and uploading a visual.

    Choose suitable dimensions, compare modern image formats, automate processing, and implement responsive delivery. Include image dimensions to prevent layout shifts, prioritize important visual elements, and test the results across different devices.

    By following these practices, developers can maintain visual quality, reduce unnecessary downloads, and create faster, more reliable website experiences.

    #10507. ‘Blue tsunami’ watch: 4 ways to track the midterm election results today

    Election Day 2026 is here. By the end of today (Tuesday, November 3, 2026), the balance of power in Washington is almost certain to have shifted. But the big question is, by how much?

    Voting in the 2026 midterm elections across the country is now underway, and most political analysts say it could be a blowout for the Democrats, with polls showing that voters are broadly concerned about the economy—especially inflationary pressures and rising gas prices.

    What do the latest polls say?

    The latest CNN Poll of Polls shows that 52% of voters prefer Democrats for Congress, compared to 43% preferring Republicans. NBC puts it at 52% for Democrats and 44% for Republicans.

    As Axios reports, election forecaster Nate Silver says the Democrats have a 95% probability of winning the House and an 80% probability of winning the Senate. More than just a “blue wave,” Silver says today’s election could be a “blue tsunami.” 

    What is the makeup of Congress right now?

    Currently, the 100 Senate seats are made up of 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats, and 2 Independents (who caucus with the Dems).

    The 435 House seats are made up of 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, and 1 Independent (with two vacancies).

    To flip both chambers, the Democrats need to achieve just 218 seats in the House and 51 in the Senate—something polls show is within reach.

    However, historically, polling has underrepresented Republican support in some states. A lot of races will also ultimately hinge on voter turnout. That means nothing is certain until every last vote is counted.

    How can I track the election results live?

    If you want to track the 2026 midterm results as they come in, you can do so online in several ways, including:

    • Maps galore: News organizations love to visualize election data, especially using maps. To see individual states turn blue or red for their open House and Senate seats tonight, you can follow along online with interactive maps from the Associated Press, Bloomberg, CNN, Fox News, and 270toWin.
    • YouTube: Cord-cutters may still prefer live broadcast coverage of election results, and for them, YouTube is a great option. Several major news outlets will be streaming their election coverage live this evening, including ABC News, CBS News, Fox News, and PBS NewsHour.
    • Google: If you don’t feel like watching talking heads or seeing maps slowly turn blue or red, and instead just want a quick update, Google is your friend. The search giant usually embeds the latest election results at the top of search result pages when you type in related queries like “election results” or “Midterm results.”
    • iPhone: Apple’s iPhone supports Live Activities—widgets that live on your home and lock screen that update in real time. Today, Apple’s News app lets people opt in to display real-time election results on their screen—no manual action required to see the latest results. To enable the Live Activity election widget, open the News app, then tap the “Follow the 2026 midterms live” banner at the top of the screen.

    Polls begin to close at 6 p.m. ET tonight, so you can expect to see the first results shortly after.

    However, if you do plan on watching all the results, you could be in for a late night. The final polls in the country—those in Alaska—don’t close until 1 a.m. ET.
